title: Dissemination of public health information during the global cholera outbreak response: WHO’s experience

chunks.text:
Since 2022, the seventh cholera pandemic has intensified globally, with cases reported to the WHO surging from 223 370 across 35 countries in 2021 to 560 823 across 60 countries in 2024.1 Reported deaths also increased significantly, going from 4159 in 2021 to 6028 in 2024. This trend continues, with preliminary data showing 562 890 cases and 5869 deaths reported across 32 countries in five regions as of 31 August 2025.2 Official figures likely underestimate the true burden due to persistent surveillance and reporting gaps. Research suggests that cholera causes between 1.3 and 4.0 million cases, and from 21 000 to 143 000 deaths annually worldwide.3
During this period, the WHO conducted 33 Rapid Risk Assessments (RRA) on country-specific and multi-country cholera outbreaks to evaluate their scale, severity and the need for an intensified response. The highest number of RRAs was published in 2022 (n=19), followed by 2021 (n=8) and 2023 (n=6). Cholera was the disease for which the highest number of RRAs was conducted each year from 2021 to 2023.4 On 26 January 2023, the rapid increase in cholera cases across multiple regions, compounded by widespread outbreaks in complex humanitarian settings, shortages of oral cholera vaccines alongside other critical supplies and insufficient operational capacity, led the WHO to classify the global resurgence of cholera as a Grade 3 emergency—the organisation’s highest emergency level.5 6 This grading triggered the activation of WHO’s Incident Management System (IMS), an organisation-wide mechanism that unites resources, expertise and processes at all levels to deliver coordinated support to affected countries.7
In accordance with the International Health Regulations (IHR),8 the WHO has provided regular epidemiological and operational updates to inform the international community about the global resurgence of cholera and enhance operational activities. From January 2021 to September 2023, the WHO published 17 Disease Outbreak News reports on the cholera situation from Africa (n=10), the Eastern Mediterranean (n=3) and the Americas (n=2), as well as two global reports each in 2022 and 2023. Following the establishment of the Incident Management Support Team (IMST), the WHO released the first multi-country outbreak external situation report on 28 March 2023.9 As of 26 September 2025, 30 editions of the monthly situation report have been published, providing comprehensive updates on the epidemiological trends and the global public health response.
The situation report is publicly accessible on the Health Emergency page of the WHO website10 and the cholera upsurge web page (2021–present).11 Between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2024, the WHO Health Emergencies Programme web page, where the cholera situation reports were published, received 3 million visits from more than 110 countries. The majority of visits came from the Region of the Americas (32%), followed by the European Region (24%), the South-East Asia Region (17%), the Western Pacific Region (16%), the African Region (7%) and the Eastern Mediterranean Region (4%). As of 8 November 2024, the situation report also had more than 15 000 downloads from the cholera upsurge web page (2021–present). The report is also available through various other channels, including the Global Task Force on Cholera Control (GTFCC)’s website12 and the humanitarian information platform ReliefWeb.13 The situation report is complemented by WHO’s Global Cholera and Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD) Dashboard,14 which delivers a monthly update on cholera cases and deaths worldwide, further enhancing transparency and situational awareness. High engagement with WHO’s cholera situation reports across web platforms strengthens global collaboration, informs decision-making and raises public awareness for effective outbreak response. This article assesses the development, execution and impact of WHO’s cholera situation reports, detailing the methodology used to ensure data accuracy and timeliness, including country selection criteria and internal validation. It highlights key challenges in obtaining cholera outbreak data and offers recommendations to strengthen collaboration, data sharing and response coordination. Information sharing during emergency response ensures timely action, reduces risks, prevents misinformation and enables efficient global collaboration for effective intervention.
chunks.heading: Introduction

chunks.text: The situation report is structured into several sections, including global and regional epidemiological overviews, with a focus on severely impacted subregions and countries. It also provides operational updates covering all response pillars. Additionally, the report highlights key challenges and outlines the next steps for managing the ongoing global cholera outbreak.
chunks.heading: Introduction > Overview of the WHO multi-country cholera outbreak situation report

chunks.text:
The report’s epidemiological updates give an in-depth analysis of the outbreak’s progression globally and by the WHO Region, focusing on recent data on reported cholera cases and deaths to track trends and highlight countries, territories or areas of concern. These updates enable the monitoring of transmission dynamics over time and across regions, offering actionable insights into the effectiveness of current control measures and highlighting areas where additional public health response efforts may be needed.
Beyond global and regional summaries, the report includes detailed analyses of subregions and countries significantly impacted by cholera, particularly where high incidence and fatality rates might coincide with other health emergencies. By highlighting these areas, the report draws attention to the challenges that may exacerbate the risk of cholera, including resource constraints, healthcare system pressures and heightened vulnerability from factors like conflict or natural disasters.
Countries that fulfil two of the following criteria are included in the situation report for in-depth discussion: experiencing cholera outbreaks with high burden of cases and mortality rates, facing concurrent public health and humanitarian emergencies, or encountering ongoing operational challenges in the cholera response. To enhance accessibility and comprehension, data are presented through various visual aids, such as tables, graphs and maps (figure 1, table 1). Maps illustrate the geographic spread of cholera, indicating areas of high incidence, while epidemiological curves show transmission trends over time. Together, these subregional and country-specific analyses, along with the accompanying visual aids, equip public health officials and policymakers with a nuanced view of the evolving cholera outbreak (figures 2 and 3).
chunks.heading: Introduction > Overview of the WHO multi-country cholera outbreak situation report > Global and regional epidemiological overviews

chunks.text:
This section summarises WHO’s collaborative work with partners at global, regional and national levels to support countries in essential pillars of the response, including coordination, surveillance,15 laboratory,16 vaccination,17 case management, infection prevention and control, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH),18 risk communication and community engagement,19 operations support and logistics, prevention and response to sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment, and preparedness and readiness.20
By presenting detailed updates on operational progress, challenges and strategic priorities across these response pillars, the Operational updates section provides a critical platform for enhanced coordination. It facilitates the alignment of resources, promotes stakeholder collaboration and ensures transparency in response efforts. Through these insights, the WHO and its partners can identify gaps, direct support more efficiently and ensure that all aspects of the response address the most urgent needs, ultimately supporting a more cohesive and impactful global effort against cholera.

title: Multi-country outbreak of cholera, epidemiological update #33 -27 January 2026

chunks.text:
Edition 33
27 January 2026
| Emergency situation update
chunks.heading: Multi-country outbreak of cholera, epidemiological update #33 -27 January 2026

chunks.text:
From 1 January to 28 December 2025, a cumulative total of 614 828 cholera cases and 7598 deaths were reported from 33 countries across five WHO regions, with the Eastern Mediterranean Region recording the highest numbers, followed by the African Region, the South-East Asia Region, the Region of the Americas, and the Western Pacific Region. No cases were reported from the European Region during this period.
In December 2025 (epidemiological weeks 49 to 52) a total of 17 327 new cholera and acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) cases were reported from 16 countries across three WHO regions, showing a 25% decrease from November. In this period, 137 cholera-related deaths were reported globally, a 16% decrease from the previous month.
Cholera upsurge (2021-present): https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/cholera-upsurge/

| Emergency situation update
chunks.heading: Multi-country outbreak of cholera, epidemiological update #34 -21 February 2026

chunks.text:
In January 2026 (epidemiological weeks 1 to 4), a total of 16 912 new cholera and acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) cases were reported from 19 countries, territories, and areas across three WHO regions, showing a 6% decrease from December 2025. The African Region registered the highest number of cases, followed by the Eastern Mediterranean Region, and the South-East Asia Region. This period also saw 182 cholera-related deaths globally, highlighting a 20% increase from the previous month. No outbreaks were reported in the Western Pacific Region or Region of the Americas during this time.

title: CDC in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

chunks.text: CDC established an office in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2002. CDC collaborates closely with the Government of DRC, the Ministry of Health (MOH), and various partners to build effective public health collaboration and partnerships to detect, prevent, and respond to global public health threats. CDC's work aims to protect the health of Americans and support public health around the world.
chunks.heading: At a glance

chunks.text:
• Pioneering electronic integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) using the DHIS2 platform in six provinces, allowing real-time surveillance reporting with integrated laboratory results, to improve the 7-1-7 model for outbreak responses in the DRC.
• Mentored 16 laboratories towards ISO 15189 accreditation, including two that became DRC’s first internationally accredited clinical laboratories in 2025. Established diagnostic capacities for HIV, monkeypox, and viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Marburg Virus Disease and Ebola), and supported installation of a lab information system in 10 laboratories to streamline operations.
• Supported the training of 925 disease detectives through the Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), trained 120 MOH staff in emergency management, and educated over 3,800 healthcare providers in malaria diagnosis and treatment.
• Deployed staff and lab equipment to the 2025 Ebola outbreak (16th Ebola outbreak in DRC) in Bulape to support surveillance and laboratory testing. Supported the Ebola Treatment Unit laboratory to perform specimen testing for patient follow up.
• Provided technical support for surveillance and tetanus vaccination campaigns that led to the elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2019.
• Contributed to the recent monkeypox and Ebola responses through laboratory testing, case investigations, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and community engagement.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Key accomplishments

chunks.text:
DRC has a large population, spans a vast geographic area, and shares borders with nine other countries. CDC, MOH, and various partners collaborate to prevent, detect, respond to, and control infectious disease outbreaks within the country.
CDC was the major partner who worked with the MOH to establish the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in 2022, which coordinates essential public health functions such as preparedness and outbreak response, surveillance, laboratory systems, and workforce development.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security

chunks.text:
CDC has successfully accredited two laboratories to ISO 15189 standards. Additionally, CDC helped develop a national laboratory strategic plan that directs the strengthening of laboratory systems in DRC. This includes donating essential equipment and enhancing laboratory diagnostics, network optimization, and quality management systems to meet the growing demand for early diagnosis of infectious diseases.
CDC also supported the installation of a laboratory information system (LIS) in 10 laboratories to streamline their processes. Furthermore, CDC has provided training for laboratory staff and monitored testing quality through an external quality assurance program.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security > Laboratory strengthening

chunks.text:
DRC’s FETP currently offers three levels of training: frontline, intermediate, and advanced. Participants enhance their skills in data collection and the translation of data into evidence-based actions. FETP graduates primarily include national and district public health staff, whose expertise has been vital in DRC’s responses to monkeypox, Ebola, COVID-19, and cholera.
CDC has supported more than 900 FETP deployers throughout the country to participate in polio surveillance, monkeypox and Ebola outbreak responses, vaccination campaigns, and other immunization activities. Through FETP, CDC strengthens DRC’s workforce capacity to identify and contain outbreaks before they escalate globally.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security > Workforce development

chunks.text:
CDC has supported Ebola outbreak responses through disease surveillance, laboratory support, border health, data management, infection prevention and control, vaccination, and risk communication and community engagement.
For DRC’s 2025 Ebola outbreak in Bulape, CDC-supported activities included:
• Deploying a mobile sequencing laboratory to perform real-time data that links cases and guides response activities.
• Sending 27 field epidemiologists to assist with case investigations and contact-tracing. Additionally, CDC headquarters subject matter experts and CDC DRC Country Office staff have deployed to Bulape to provide technical assistance for the response.
• Digitalizing and harmonizing data by deploying and expanding the DHIS2 in Kasai and neighboring provinces to enhance real time data reporting and analysis.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Ebola

chunks.text:
CDC has provided support for monkeypox research and response in DRC for over 20 years. DRC declared a monkeypox outbreak in 2022, which was classified as a public health emergency of international concern in August 2024. As of October 2025, the country has reported approximately 100,000 monkeypox cases. CDC is actively assisting the MOH with the response including surveillance, laboratory capacity, and workforce. The deployment of 50 to 70 field epidemiologists in hotspot provinces has been instrumental in mitigating the outbreak.
CDC collaborated to assess the effectiveness of the monkeypox vaccine (MBA-BN), used in an endemic zone in 1,600 health care workers in 6 health zones of Tshuapa province. The study showed an effective antibody response in 99% of recipients for up to 5 years.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Monkeypox

chunks.text:
As a key implementer of the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), CDC plays an essential role in the fight against HIV and TB. With unmatched scientific and technical knowledge and long-standing relationships with ministries of health, CDC is uniquely positioned to advance HIV, TB, and other global health security activities that keep Americans safe at home and abroad.
Through PEPFAR, CDC provides critical support to DRC's public health infrastructure, improving the country's ability to prevent, detect, and respond to HIV, TB, and other infectious diseases and minimizing their risk from entering the U.S.
chunks.heading: At a glance > HIV and TB

chunks.text:
CDC supports the MOH in the distribution and mass vaccination campaigns for new vaccines. CDC also works to improve outbreak detection, and enhance disease surveillance systems and reduce their impact on human health and economies.
CDC’s immunization-related support to DRC reduces the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases and lowers the risk of disease transmission beyond the country’s borders, thereby protecting the U.S. and safeguarding Americans.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Immunization

chunks.text:
DRC continues to experience cholera outbreaks, driven by poor sanitation, limited access to clean water, and ongoing conflict. CDC provides technical assistance to MOH, focusing on improving surveillance, outbreak response, and laboratory capacities.
Additionally, CDC has funded a partner to implement essential water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) initiatives aimed at reducing cholera transmission by enhancing access to safe drinking water, promoting hygiene practices, and ensuring adequate sanitation facilities for vulnerable populations.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Cholera

chunks.text:
CDC has collaborated with partners to support implementation of malaria prevention and control activities in DRC.
CDC-supported activities have included providing technical input in:
• Monitoring mosquito behavior and resistance to insecticides.
• Providing long-lasting insecticide-treated bed nets.
• Preventing malaria during pregnancy.
• Enhancing diagnostics, surveillance, and evaluation of malaria-related activities.
• Researching social and behavioral changes impacting malaria prevention and case management.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Malaria

chunks.text: With financial and technical support from CDC, DRC began influenza surveillance in 2006. Currently, four sentinel sites conduct influenza surveillance in DRC's capital of Kinshasa. Influenza surveillance is focused among patients with influenza-like illness or severe acute respiratory illness. These activities formed the backbone for conducting COVID-19 surveillance in DRC.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Influenza

chunks.text: CDC has worked in Zambia since 2000. CDC Zambia works closely with the Government of Zambia, Ministry of Health, Zambia National Public Health Institute, and other partner organizations to prevent, detect, respond to infectious disease outbreaks and support broader disease control efforts for HIV and TB. CDC’s work aims to protect the health of Americans and public health around the world.
chunks.heading: At a glance

chunks.text:
• Supported development and deployment of SmartCare, a national electronic medical record system for patient and program monitoring, to over 1,600 clinics nationwide.
• Supported national and subnational laboratories to achieve international standard accreditation and built government capacity to perform to detect outbreaks through the National Multi-Pathogen Detection Program.
• Supported training of 501 fellows from the Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), many of whom now support key public health roles at the national and subnational level.
• Expanded the Extension for Community Health Outcomes program, which allows Zambian experts to lend clinical expertise and provide consultations to over 500 sites across all of Zambia’s 10 provinces.
• Pioneered the government to government (G2G) model, where subnational authorities receive direct funding from CDC to implement health programs, and approach that improves outcomes and saves costs.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Key accomplishments

chunks.text: CDC’s global health security work in Zambia focuses on strengthening the country’s public health systems across the following core areas:
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security

chunks.text:
CDC supports public health systems strengthening in Zambia by engaging in:
• Enhancement of epidemiology, disease and mortality surveillance, program monitoring, and health information systems, including SmartCare, DHIS2, and Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR).
• Establishment and continued support of the National Public Health Institute to strengthen public health surveillance and the capacities to prepare for, detect, and respond to health threats, including viral hemorrhagic fevers, such as Ebola, which are endemic in neighboring countries.
• Evaluations to assess program impact and inform rapid adjustments to address the evolving HIV, TB, and emerging disease epidemics.
• Support of the Government of Zambia to lead public health responses.
• Support of local government, at the provincial and district level, to provide health services.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security > Public health systems

chunks.text: CDC supports training disease detectives through FETP. The program trains professionals to perform disease surveillance and contain outbreaks of infectious diseases that can quickly become . FETP trainees learn critical skills for data collection and analysis and using data to inform action. CDC also supports the expansion of academic and clinical training programs in the University of Zambia and the University Teaching Hospital and the use of the Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) platform to enhance training and mentorship.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security > Workforce development

chunks.text: CDC works to strengthen the capacity of Zambia's emergency response. During various outbreaks, from COVID-19 to cholera, CDC Zambia has supported vaccination campaigns, disease surveillance strategy, contact tracing, and laboratory testing.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Global health security > Emergency response

chunks.text:
As a key implementer of the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), CDC plays an essential role in the fight against HIV and TB. With unmatched scientific and technical knowledge and long-standing relationships with ministries of health, CDC is uniquely positioned to advance HIV, TB, and other global health security activities that keep Americans safe at home and abroad.
Through PEPFAR, CDC provides critical support to Zambia's public health infrastructure, improving the country's ability to prevent, detect, and respond to HIV, TB, and other infectious diseases and minimizing their risk from entering the U.S.
chunks.heading: At a glance > HIV and TB

chunks.text: CDC Zambia has a longstanding collaboration with the University Teaching Hospital and Ministry of Health on influenza surveillance projects. The findings from these collaborative activities help the U.S. to better understand trends and emerging threats from influenza and other diseases with pandemic potential in Zambia and the Southern Africa region. In addition, specimens from influenza program contribute to a global initiative that uses information on strains in the Southern Hemisphere to design the seasonal influenza vaccine for the U.S.–improving prevention efforts for at-risk Americans and saving lives.
chunks.heading: At a glance > Influenza
